title: The BST property
sub: Bounds from the ancestors versus in-order, and why comparing with children is not enough
cards/0/title: The problem and the BST property
cards/0/body:
Validate Binary Search Tree (LeetCode #98). Given the root of a binary tree, check that it is a binary search tree (BST): for every node, all keys in its left subtree are strictly less than the node’s key, all keys in its right subtree are strictly greater, and both subtrees are BSTs too. There are 1 to 10⁴ nodes, and the values span the whole int range, from −2³¹ to 2³¹ − 1.

The property is about whole subtrees, not children. Everything a BST is good for rests on it: a search follows one branch and costs O(h), the minimum is the leftmost node, and the walk “left subtree, node, right subtree” yields the keys in ascending order.

Example: [2, 1, 3] is a BST. [5, 1, 4, null, null, 3, 6] is not: 4 lies in the right subtree of 5, and 4 < 5.
cards/1/title: Naive: compare with the children — and why it is wrong
cards/1/body:
The first idea: at every node check that the left child is smaller and the right child is larger, then go down. The code is short, O(n) — and wrong: it checks children, while the property is about the whole subtree. On [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] node 6 has children 3 and 7, everything looks fine locally, but 3 lies in the right subtree of 5 and is smaller than 5. This is the main trap of the problem, and the interviewer expects you to come up with such a counterexample yourself.

The honest naive solution: for every node find the maximum of the left subtree and the minimum of the right one and compare them with the node. It is correct, but every subtree is walked again for each of its ancestors: O(n·h), O(n²) on a chain — on the order of 5·10⁷ steps for n = 10⁴.

We need every node checked once, but against all of its ancestors.
cards/2/q: The tree [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20]. What does the “children only” check return, and what is actually true?
cards/2/options/0: It returns true, but this is not a BST: 6 lies in the right subtree of 10
cards/2/options/1: It returns false: 6 is less than 15
cards/2/options/2: It returns true, and this is a BST: every node’s left child is smaller and right child larger
cards/2/explain: 10 has children 5 and 15, 15 has 6 and 20: every parent–child pair is in order, so the check returns true. But 6 lies to the right of 10, and the whole right subtree of 10 must be greater than 10. A local check cannot see violations that skip a level.
cards/2/wrong/1: 6 is the left child of 15, and 6 < 15: for a left child that is exactly right.
cards/2/wrong/2: The BST property is about the whole subtree: 6 cannot appear to the right of 10, at any depth.
cards/3/body:
Every ancestor constrains a node. Go left from an ancestor and the node must be smaller than it; go right and it must be larger. All the constraints along the path collapse into one open interval (lo, hi): lo is the nearest ancestor we went right from, hi is the nearest one we went left from.

So the recursion carries the interval down. The root gets (−∞, +∞); the left child of a node gets (lo, node.val) — the top narrows; the right child gets (node.val, hi) — the bottom narrows. Invariant: the tree is a BST if and only if every node lies strictly inside the interval that came from above. Every node is checked once: O(n) time, O(h) stack. The && gives an early exit: if the left subtree is broken, the right one is never walked.

How to represent ∞. The values span the whole int, so int.MinValue cannot play “−∞”: a node with the value int.MinValue would fail the “greater than lo” check. Keep the bounds in long — long.MinValue is strictly less than any int — or in int?, where null means “no bound”.
cards/4/explain: The root’s lower bound is long.MinValue: it is strictly less than any int, so a node holding int.MinValue passes. An empty subtree violates nothing — true. Equality is forbidden on both sides, hence <= lo and >= hi. Going left, the top narrows to node.val; going right, the bottom becomes node.val and the top stays the same hi.
cards/5/task: Step through the check on [5, 3, 8, 1, 6, 7, 9]. Each checked node is labelled with its interval. The rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: 3 ∈ (−∞, 5) — fine. The next node is 1, the left child of 3. Which interval does it get?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: Going left narrows the top: the upper bound of 1 is its parent’s value, 3, and the bottom stays what came to 3, which is −∞. The bound 5 still applies, but 3 is tighter: (−∞, 3) lies entirely inside (−∞, 5).
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: 6 is outside (3, 5) — not a BST, the walk stops
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: 6 is larger than its parent 3 — the right child is fine
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: 1 is fine and has no children. Next is 6, the right child of 3. What does the check say?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: 6 receives the interval (3, 5): the bottom is its parent 3 (we went right), the top is the root 5 (this whole subtree is on its left). 6 > 5 — a violation. Against its parent 6 compares fine, so the “children only” check would miss it. && keeps the walk out of the root’s right subtree: the answer is already false.
cards/6/title: In-order: a BST reads in ascending order
cards/6/body:
The second approach uses a consequence of the property: an in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits a BST in strictly ascending order. So the tree is a BST if and only if every next in-order value is greater than the previous one. No need to store the whole list — a single prev is enough.

In-order is convenient to write without recursion, on an explicit stack: go left as far as possible pushing nodes; pop the top one — it is the next in ascending order; move into its right subtree. The stack holds at most h nodes: O(n) time, O(h) memory, and an early exit at the first neighbouring pair that does not increase.

The bound trap is the same: starting with int prev = int.MinValue breaks on a tree whose leftmost value is int.MinValue. Start with long prev = long.MinValue, or keep TreeNode prev = null and compare only once it is set.
cards/7/q: On the tree [-2147483648, null, 5] this code returns false, although the tree is a BST. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: The root, int.MinValue, is the first node popped in-order, and int.MinValue <= prev = int.MinValue — a false violation. “Less than everything” cannot be represented by a value from the same range. One line fixes it: long prev = long.MinValue (or TreeNode prev = null with a check). The <= comparison itself is right: duplicates are not allowed in this problem’s BST.
cards/8/q: What is true about the bounds solution and the in-order solution? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: Both are O(n) time and O(h) memory
cards/8/options/1: In-order finds a violation at the first pair of neighbouring values that does not increase
cards/8/options/2: The children-only check is correct if the tree is balanced
cards/8/options/3: A node holding int.MinValue breaks the solution with long bounds
cards/8/options/4: If the root’s left subtree is broken, the bounds solution does not walk the right one
cards/8/explain: Both visit every node once, and the stack — call stack or explicit — holds a path no longer than h. In-order compares neighbours in ascending order: the first pair with prev ≥ val is the violation. Balance is irrelevant: [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20] is balanced, and the children check still gets it wrong. long.MinValue is less than any int, so int.MinValue passes. && does not evaluate its right side when the left one is already false.
cards/9/title: SortedSet: a BST that does not degenerate
cards/9/body:
A plain BST without balancing depends on the insertion order. Insert keys 1, 2, …, n in ascending order and each goes to the right of the previous one: the tree becomes a chain, h = n, a search is O(n), n inserts are O(n²). It is easy to get there by accident, for example by inserting enemy ids in spawn order.

A balanced tree fixes its shape with rotations after every insert and removal and keeps h = O(log n). SortedSet<T> and SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> in .NET are a red-black tree (see the collections lesson in the first unit): h ≤ 2·log₂(n + 1), O(log n) operations in the worst case. That is the answer to “how is SortedSet built”: a BST with this lesson’s property plus balancing.

The in-order walk is the same here: foreach over a SortedSet yields elements in ascending order because its enumerator is an in-order walk on an explicit stack. The k-th smallest element of a BST (#230) is the same walk with a counter: stop at the k-th popped node, O(h + k).
cards/9/deep:
Inside the SortedSet enumerator. In the dotnet/runtime sources, SortedSet<T>.Enumerator is a struct, but its constructor creates a Stack<Node> with capacity 2·log₂(n + 1) — the maximum height of a red-black tree. So foreach over a SortedSet allocates a stack (an object and an array) even when the enumerator is not boxed — noticeable in a hot Unity loop. The internal InOrderTreeWalk works the same way.

Red-black versus AVL. AVL keeps the height difference of subtrees at most 1 — the tree is lower (about 1.44·log₂ n), lookups are slightly faster, but updates rotate more. Red-black allows height up to 2·log₂(n + 1), but an insert does at most two rotations and a removal at most three. Standard libraries (.NET, Java’s TreeMap, std::map in common implementations) choose red-black.

Unity and Burst. SortedSet is available in the .NET Standard 2.1 profile, but every node is a heap object: an allocation on every Add and cache misses on the way down. The com.unity.collections package has no balanced search tree; in Jobs you usually sort a NativeList<T> and binary-search it, and when the data rarely changes that is faster than a tree anyway.
cards/10/q: A hand-written BST without balancing. Enemies get ascending ids — 1, 2, 3, … — and are inserted in spawn order, 10⁵ in total. What about the cost?
cards/10/options/0: The tree is a chain: the inserts cost about 5·10⁹ steps, Contains is O(n)
cards/10/options/1: O(n log n) for all inserts: a BST search is always logarithmic
cards/10/options/2: O(n): a new id always lands right of the previous one, so an insert is O(1)
cards/10/explain: Every new id is larger than all previous ones and goes to the far right end: the tree degenerates into a chain, h = n. The i-th insert walks i nodes, about n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹ steps in total. The cure is balancing — SortedSet<int> gives O(log n) — or a dictionary if order does not matter.
cards/10/wrong/1: Only a balanced tree is logarithmic. The height of a hand-written BST depends on the insertion order.
cards/10/wrong/2: An insert starts at the root and walks down the whole chain: a BST has no pointer to its last node.
cards/11/q: You are solving Validate BST out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: strictly less and greater or not, are there duplicates, what is the value range
cards/11/items/1: Name the trap: comparing only with children misses violations across levels — counterexample [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7]
cards/11/items/2: Idea: pass the interval (lo, hi) from the ancestors down
cards/11/items/3: Write the code with long bounds, saying: going left narrows hi, going right narrows lo
cards/11/items/4: Run the counterexample: 3 gets (5, 6) and fails
cards/11/items/6: Edge cases: int.MinValue and int.MaxValue in nodes, a single node, a chain
cards/11/explain: The problem, then a counterexample to the obvious solution — it shows you understand the property — then the idea, the code and a run on that same counterexample. Complexity and edge cases go last; int.MinValue is not a detail here but the reason to use long.
cards/12/q: Match the problem or question with the answer.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: Interval (lo, hi) passed down from ancestors
cards/12/pairs/1/0: Walk a BST in ascending order
cards/12/pairs/3/0: “−∞” when values span the whole int
